steps.observation: You have 60 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn had been silent for three days when the voices began.

Elias found them first in the logbook, crowding the margins in a tight, unfamiliar hand. He had been halfway through noting the noon weather—“Visibility poor, wind easterly”—when extra words glimmered faintly between his own:

you are not alone

The ink was the same blue, the strokes as neat as his, but he hadn’t written them. He checked the door’s deadbolt twice, then climbed the spiral stairs of Greyhook Light, listening for footsteps that were not his own.

The lighthouse rose from its rock like a finger of bone, five miles off a coast that had forgotten it. Once, ships had depended on this tower; now their lights passed far out at sea, guided by satellites and signals that never tasted salt. The world had outgrown Greyhook, but Elias remained—part habit, part stubbornness, part quiet fear of what waited ashore in the noisy century he did not understand.

At the lantern room, the great glass eye turned with its slow, unhurried grace. The lamp was modern, reliable, a cold brilliance at odds with the rusted rails and peeling paint. Elias circled once, checking bolts and glass panels. Nothing: just the revolving beam sweeping the emptiness, carving a pale path across endless water.

He went back down. The wind moaned around the stone, a constant, wordless complaint. In the kitchen, the kettle began to chatter on the stove. As he reached for it, he noticed the condensation on the window—four letters traced in the steam.

stay

He froze, his breath frosting the pane. Slowly, with a fingertip that trembled more from age than fear, he wiped the word away.

“Who’s there?” he asked the empty kitchen.

Only the sea answered, hurling itself against the rock far below.

For the rest of the day he moved mechanically through his rounds. Oil levels. Battery checks. Lantern cleaning. Every now and then his eye snagged on some surface that might bear writing—the brass of the barometer, the chalkboard with its weekly tide tables, the whitewashed stairwell. He found nothing. By evening, he had almost convinced himself of a momentary lapse, a trick of exhaustion.

Night came early, pressed down by thick, unbroken cloud. The light’s familiar sweep washed through the fog, a heartbeat made of glass and flame. Elias took his supper in the watchroom: tinned soup, bread hardened at the edges, an apple. Rain ticked on the windows. The radio, its innards older than many of the ships nearby, whispered dead air.

He opened the logbook again.

Page after page, his own careful script marched in orderly lines. Weather, maintenance, the rare call with the supply boat. Then, on yesterday’s entry, between “15:32 – sighted trawler to northwest” and his initials, a thin line of text had woven itself like a seam.

don’t go

The pen lifted from his hand. For the first time in years, Elias considered leaving the sentence unfinished. Instead he added, in letters a little too stiff:

“17:10 – possible unknown interference with log.”

He closed the book firmly.

The wind rose as the night deepened. The foghorn, automated now, woke in its concrete throat and bellowed at the dark. Elias paced the circumference of the watchroom until the familiar aches settled in his knees and back, grounding him. Eventually, he doused the smaller lamps and let the revolving beacon be the room’s only heartbeat.

He slept in fits, in the narrow iron bed squeezed into the lowest room. When he woke—abruptly, with the sensation of having been spoken to—there was no sound but the rush of waves and the rhythmic grind of the lens above.

Elias realized he was clutching something. Slowly, he opened his fist.

A folded scrap of paper, edges straight as if torn from nothing at all.

His name was written on the outside in his own hand.

With fingers gone suddenly clumsy, he unfolded it.

PLEASE

The word was written once, in shaky letters, then again, firmer, then a third time, as neat and level as any log entry. Below the third, as if the writer had finally found their balance, a full sentence appeared.

Please don’t extinguish me.

He read it three times. The paper was dry, warm from his own grasp. No seams of ink bled through. No impression marked the underside. It felt as though the words simply were.

It was ridiculous. He was a man of mechanical things, of lenses and fuel and the known behavior of storms. He knew precisely when the light had gone out, each time power had failed across the years. Metal did not speak. Glass did not plead.

And yet, thirty miles down the coast, a new automated beacon glared from a reinforced tower, bright and tireless and connected to everything he was not. Two months ago a letter had come in the supply boat, wrapped in plastic against the spray.

Decommissioning, they called it.

“The ceremony is scheduled for next Tuesday at 12:00 hours. Light will be extinguished at 12:05. Your transfer paperwork to the mainland station is enclosed.”

He had folded the letter back into its envelope and placed it under the sugar tin, the way one hid mouse traps.

Now, in the light of the single bulb that swung gently with the tower’s subtle sway, he held this impossible plea between fingers that smelled faintly of oil and salt.

“Who are you?” he asked the empty room.

The kettle did not answer. The walls, long-accustomed to holding back storms, said nothing. His own breath sounded too loud in his ears.

He dressed as if for morning rounds, though the clock on the wall insisted it was still hours before dawn. The routine steadied him: thick socks, boots laced tight, sweater, old pea coat that had once been navy blue. He slipped the folded paper into his pocket and climbed.

The ascent through the lighthouse’s throat was a spiral of familiar ghosts. Here, the chip in the stone where a crate had been dropped his first month. There, the nail he had hammered in for a lantern during the winter the generator failed. The walls smelled of salt and old paint, a layered memory of storms survived.

At the top, he unlocked the lantern room and stepped into the turning light.

Out there, the fog was absolute, a blanketing presence that devoured everything beyond the glass. The beam pushed through it, a pale, insistent finger, sweeping the darkness in its patient arc. Every turn, every pulse, felt like a breath.

He rested his hands on the metal railing that circled the great lens.

“They’re replacing you,” he said softly to the machinery. “You know that.”

The light continued its slow revolution, as if in answer.

Elias reached into his pocket and unfolded the paper again, placing it on the narrow ledge by the maintenance log.

“I don’t choose these things,” he said. Salt stung his throat, though there was no spray up here. “They send their letters. They send their boats. They take the oil away, bring in new bulbs. Now they take you, too.”

The glass panes rattled as a gust struck them. For a moment the light’s beam faltered, refracted strangely in the swirl. The hairs on his arms lifted, as if the air itself had taken a breath.

He remembered the early years, when every night was crowded with lights—trawlers, freighters, the slow, dignified passage of liners. Their horns called back and forth across the water, and sometimes, just sometimes, one would answer the lighthouse’s beam with a prolonged flash, a silent greeting. On those nights, when the sea was more voice than threat, he had felt...not proud, exactly, but necessary.

Over time, the ships had edged farther out, their routes shifting. Their lights became rare visitors. Greyhook’s beam rotated on, its circle faithful, diminishing audience be damned.

“Who are you?” he asked again, but this time not to the empty room.

The light’s reflection caught his eyes in the glass, pale and small compared to the great, patient lens.

Ink bloomed across the paper beside his hand, as if the fibers themselves had decided to darken.

keeper, came the first word. Then: anchor. Then, as if searching, a series of halting phrases.

i am the turning  
i am the watching  
i am the waiting for return

The letters wavered, then steadied.

i am the light

Elias’s legs folded him onto the low stool before his body could decide whether to flee. He pressed his palms flat against his knees to stop their trembling.

“If you’re the light,” he said slowly, “then you’ve been alone here almost as long as I have.”

The pen that lay unused on the ledge rolled, just slightly, toward him.

you stayed, appeared on the paper.

“For a wage,” Elias said automatically, then shook his head at his own lie. “For habit. For...not knowing where else to go.”

you stayed, it repeated, as if the nuance were irrelevant.

you turn me  
you clean my glass  
you tell the world i am here

He swallowed. The storm outside worried at the glass, unappeased.

“They don’t need you anymore,” he said. “Not like they did.”

i need you, wrote the light.

The simplicity of it cut him more cleanly than any wave-worn rock ever had.

Far below, where the tower met stone, the sea made its constant, grinding threat. Wind sang in the guy wires, an old, high sound. The machinery hummed, electricity tracing the same circuits it always had.

“Next Tuesday,” Elias said. “They’ll come to shut you down. Ceremony, they call it. Speeches on the radio, if anyone cares to listen. The new beacon down the coast will…will see to things.”

Silence, except for the turn and click, turn and click of the great lens.

please, the paper said. then:

is it dark where they will send you

He thought of the mainland station: windowless, he’d heard, full of screens and blinking lights. No salt in the air. No real horizon, only digital representations of one. Shifts measured not by sun or storm but by clock and calendar. A hum of machines that had never been rained on.

“Different,” he said.

dark, the paper insisted.          

He almost protested, then let his shoulders sag. “Yes,” he said. “Dark, in the way that matters.”

The light’s beam swept the fog in unbroken rhythm. Elias became suddenly aware of how tired he was. Not the layered fatigue of years, but a precise exhaustion that belonged to this single, impossible conversation.

“What would you have me do?” he whispered.

stay, the paper wrote, as if there were no other word.

The supply boat would come. The officials in their bright jackets would climb his stairs and shake his hand firmly, the way men did when they were closing something. They would throw switches. They would declare Greyhook Light retired, a relic. They would take him away.

“You’re asking me to defy orders,” he said, because it was easier than admitting the smaller, truer fear: You’re asking me to admit that you are real.

you already defy time, the light wrote, letters steady now. every night you kindle me when the world has brighter things. every day you keep watch when no one looks back.

Thunder rolled far off, a low, delayed reply. The room brightened and dimmed with the revolving beam.

Elias thought of his first night here, decades ago, standing uncertain in this very room, hands too clean not yet scented with oil, the old keeper watching him with pale, assessing eyes.

“It’s not the lamp that keeps them safe,” that man had said, tapping the glass. “It’s the knowing someone is tending it. Light left alone goes bad. Forgets what it’s for.”

At the time, Elias had dismissed it as an old man’s superstition, the kind that grows like moss in isolated places. Yet here he was, half a lifetime later, speaking to something that had learned to write itself into margins and steam.

“What happens to you when they put you out?” he asked.

There was a long pause. For a moment, he thought the conversation had been a kind of waking dream. Then, slowly:

i turn no more  
i see no more  
i wait   
and nothing answers

He imagined the lens, motionless. The glass fogged from within with dust. The slow encroachment of spiderwebs. The sea erasing their shared routines wave by wave.

He imagined, to his surprise, himself elsewhere: in a control room he had never seen, watching electronic dots move on a screen. Telling himself that safety was just as real when it passed through fiber-optic cables. Telling himself that near enough was enough.

The paper shivered beneath his hand as the tower took another gust.

“There’s a law,” he said, though the words felt thin. “Contracts. Regulations. Progress.”

Above them, the lamp burned with unwavering light.

Down the coastline, a new beacon cut its own path through the storm, bright, impersonal, tethered to systems that would not know hunger or loneliness or gratitude.

“What if I stayed?” Elias asked the question as if testing its weight for the first time, though it had been coiled in him since the envelope slid under the sugar tin. “What if I refused to go?”

He saw the practicalities instantly. The supply boat would come more rarely, if at all. The pay would stop. Repairs would become scavenging. On clear nights he might see the mainland’s smear of light and know it did not expect his return.

But he also saw other things. Morning fog parted by a beam still in motion. Nights where only one light answered his, but that answer would be enough. A stone tower that did not go dark just because someone, somewhere, had decided it was time.

you would be alone, the light wrote.  

He thought of the bed downstairs, narrow but familiar. The logbook, half-filled. The kettle, the chipped blue cup, the way the first beam of evening always found the same spot on the floorboards.

He rested his palm flat on the rail, feeling the faint vibration of the turning gear.

“I’m not,” he said.

The paper remained blank for a full revolution of the light. Then, carefully:

no

The letters steadied, bold for the first time.

you are not

Morning seeped gradually into the fog, smudging the darkness from black into grey. By the time the sun had climbed somewhere above the unbroken cloud, the sea below was a dull, heaving pewter. The beam that had once shone like a promise now glowed less brightly in the thick daylight, but it turned still, unhurried.

Elias descended to the kitchen.

He took the envelope from beneath the sugar tin and opened it. He unfolded the letter on the table and read each line, each polite directive. Then he opened the drawer by the stove, took out the box of matches he kept for storms, and held one over the page.

He hesitated only once, as the match’s head rasped into flame.

“Progress,” he murmured, watching the paper curl and blacken, “can learn to share.”

He dropped the burning edge into the metal sink and watched until nothing but ash remained.

When the supply boat came three days later, the sea was calm, as if in cooperation with official schedules. Three men in bright jackets climbed the path. Elias met them at the base of the tower.

“You ready, Mr. Kellan?” the one in front asked, cheerful. “Big day. Last flash and all.”

“Changed my mind,” Elias said.

They laughed, then saw he was serious.

There were arguments, legal phrases, assurances of comfortable quarters on the mainland. Elias listened, hands in his coat pockets, the folded scrap of the light’s plea a small, solid presence against his fingers.

“Greyhook’s done its duty,” one of them said, turning to gesture at the distant, gleaming shape of the new beacon. “We’ve got better coverage now than ever. No need to waste resources on sentiment.”

Elias glanced up at his tower. High above, even in daylight, the lens turned. Its shadow moved across the stone like a heartbeat.

“You see waste,” he said quietly. “I see a promise no one told the sea had expired.”

They threatened to report him. They promised to return with papers and perhaps a uniformed man or two. He nodded at each, as if accepting the inevitability of weather.

When their boat’s engine noise had faded, he climbed back up to the lantern room.

He laid his palm against the glass, now warm with the effort of shining into a day that barely needed it.

“They’ll keep trying,” he said.

On the maintenance ledge, where no breeze could reach, the scrap of paper shook once, then lay still. Ink formed with patient deliberation.

we will keep turning

He smiled, a slow, surprised thing that reached places in his face that had forgotten how.

Outside, far off, a freighter moved along the horizon, content in its satellite-guided path, but as Greyhook’s beam brushed its flank, one small light blinked twice in answer.

Elias watched that distant glimmer and felt the tower around him settle, stone and metal and man and something that was neither and both. The world would go on growing brighter in ways that did not need him. Let it.

Here, on this stubborn rock, a light would continue to sweep the waters, tended and tending, not because someone far inland had decreed it should, but because two old keepers—one of flesh, one of flame—refused to forget what they were for.
